newsitem.title: RUSSIA: De Beers says gems held at Russian airport.
newsitem.headline: De Beers says gems held at Russian airport.

text.p: Russian diamonds due to be exported and worth around $150 million are being held up by Russian customs officials for inspection, an official for De Beers of South Africa, which owns the diamonds, said on Monday.

"At the moment the diamonds are under the inspection of customs," said Raymond Clarke, head of the Moscow office of De Beers. "What is being said in the press is that the value of the diamonds is around $150 million. That's not far from the truth."
Clarke said the diamonds were held up at Moscow's Sheremetevo airport.
De Beers bought the diamonds during the first five months of the year, and wanted to export them before the end of May, when a government decree allowing gem exports runs out.
Gem exports from Russia had been blocked until last month, when the government finally issued a decree outlining export quotas until the end of May.
Another decree will be signed in the next few days outlining exports for the rest of 1997, First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said on Friday.
Clarke said the diamonds had been submitted for export before the May deadline.
"We believe the important thing is that the diamonds were logged in by a certain date, and that the cut-off date should therefore not apply," Clarke said.
He added that De Beers was cooperating with customs to resolve the problem.

De Beers and Russia's dominant diamond producer Almazy Rossii-Sakha (ARS) are awaiting the government's final seal of approval on a long-delayed gem trade deal, the draft of which was submitted to the cabinet in October last year.
Chubais said that the trade deal with De Beers would also be signed in the next few days.
"I stopped speculating a long time ago when the deal might be signed," Clarke said.
He said De Beers continued to work with ARS despite delays in signing the trade deal.
"Work is carrying on with ARS on the assumption that the deal will be signed," he said. "This will mean a minimum of delay when the document is signed," he said.
Russia accounts for about 20 percent of De Beers' Central Selling Organisation sales of rough diamonds. De Beers controls about 75 percent of the $4.5 billion annual world trade in uncut gems.
